title: Nolia: making a home on the Odisha coast
description: Nolia histories on the Odisha coast: regional names, Telugu-speaking families, remembered origins and the shared work of the shore.
lead: A community’s history can live in the languages spoken at home, the knowledge needed at sea and the relationships that make a shore a workplace. For Odisha’s Nolia communities, these connections reveal more than a single story of arrival.
author: Ahimanikya Satapathy

sections.title: A name with more than one community behind it

paragraphs.text: In a coastal study published in 1985, M. H. Kalavathy explains that people locally called Noliyas belonged to two Telugu-origin fishing communities: Jalaris and Vodabalijas. Her southern Odisha account places Jalari settlements chiefly in Ganjam and describes Vodabalija settlements extending towards Puri and the southern part of then-Cuttack district. The name therefore needs a location and a source; it cannot safely be treated as one caste with one genealogy.

The study’s southern sample comprised four villages, one Jalari and three Vodabalija. Its account connects settlement with fishing, fish marketing and local councils. These are observations of particular communities at that time, not occupations or social rules prescribed for their descendants.

Asking why this community was “created” would miss the historical problem. The available evidence describes communities moving, settling and organising their work. It does not identify a single founder or an act that created everyone known as Nolia.

sections.title: Telugu at home, a sense of belonging to Odisha

paragraphs.text: Priya Gupta’s 2010 working paper compares a predominantly Noliya fishing village in Ganjam’s Chatrapur block with a nearby agricultural settlement. The fishing families spoke Telugu, but could no longer say when their group had first settled there. That uncertainty is part of the record; a precise migration year cannot be supplied in its place.

Gupta records younger villagers studying through Odia and English, while many residents also spoke Odia. Despite the difference in language, the fishing community expressed a strong sense of belonging to Odisha rather than Andhra Pradesh. Her account shows attachment to place alongside language and occupational ties. It describes one study setting, not the views of every family today.

This is a useful starting point for thinking about Odia heritage. A history of Odisha can recognise Telugu-speaking families’ lives and contributions without erasing their language. Local belonging and a wider coastal inheritance can be held together.

sections.title: An origin tradition is a different kind of history

paragraphs.text: The Ganjam district gazetteer records a Jalandhara descent tradition associated with the Jalarulu group. It also describes migration from the south. The tradition explains belonging in a different register from a dated settlement record: it does not prove ancestry or establish when a caste formed.

The same account describes Narasingha Swamy worship at Dola Purnima and a connection with Simhachalam, citing the 1961 Nuagolabandh village monograph. This is an older reported local practice. It offers a question for family and community histories, rather than a statement that every Nolia household follows the same customs now.

sections.title: The shore is part of the working village

paragraphs.text: Dakshin Foundation’s 2021 report began with a scoping exercise in June 2019 across selected Ganjam settlements, including Sana Nolia Nuagaon. Its detailed participatory mapping centred on nearby Purnabandha. The report describes Nolia Nuagaon fishers using Purnabandha’s landing spaces; women from both settlements dried fish in the jetty building when fishing operations were not using it.

Work also connected villages through institutions. Nolia Nuagaon had a fishing committee that dealt with fisheries officials and grievances about damaged boats and nets. It belonged to the wider Maa Ganga Devi Fishing Society, which addressed disputes between member villages. Shared use did not mean agreement on everything: Nolia Nuagaon and Purnabandha fishers differed over a proposed jetty and its possible effects on the river mouth.

These examples make the shore’s role concrete. Drying space, landing access and ways of resolving disagreements are part of the conditions in which skills can be passed on. A heritage account needs to notice that everyday work as well as festivals.

The next questions belong close to families: which places do elders remember, which words name boats and gear, and who taught the skills? Accounts from Jalari and Vodabalija households should retain their own names and differences. Recording them could clarify the history without requiring descendants to remain in an inherited occupation.
